Since the exact daughter product concentrations evolve over time and can be altered by processing, no attempt was made to account for them separately in this study. The primary source of expected deviation of composition from the nominal, comes from the initial charge preparation. The U was cleaned in nitric acid prior to use to minimize surface oxide, the Mo (rolled sheet) was cleaned with acetone to remove surface contamination, and nitrile gloves were used for all material handling to protect the metals from oils and moisture. The scale used to weigh out the charges has a precision of 0.1 g. The buttons produced were each approximately 500 g, but regardless of the individual mass, ratios of components were correct within the precision of the scale. Yearly professional calibration and every-day-of-use checks (prior to and following measurements) are performed using calibrated standard masses to prevent or monitor drift. The threshold for removal from service is a calibration weight check that deviates by 0.3 g. Therefore, all measured masses can be assumed to be accurate within ±0.25 g, accounting for rounding, assuming a worst case scenario. Scale check logs from the periods of time when the buttons were produced never exceeded 0.1 g deviation during a daily check. Assuming a mischarge of 0.25 g of opposing error while weighing the Mo and U components would lead to ~0.1 wt.% deviation from nominal. Assuming losses or gains during melting occur due to a single pure component transfer (in the form of splatter from a poorly controlled arc) to a neighboring pocket (cross contamination) or out of the hearth entirely, this would add an additional ~0.2 wt.% of maximum error per gram of difference. Segregation within buttons can be possible due to the fast and highly directional nature of solidification in a water cooled hearth. While this variable cannot be controlled well by the operator, chemical sampling is performed in spatially separated (top and bottom) regions to capture maximum differences in chemistry due to this effect. Typically, impurities are limited to those which already are present in the charge materials with a couple of well known exceptions. The use of a water cooled copper hearth could be a source of copper either due to diffusion or incipient surface melting. Surface melting is rare and leaves quite obvious physical evidence of its occurrence in the hearth surface. Diffusion tends to be limited due to the relatively low (at least in relation to the melt/arc region) temperature of the copper hearth interface due to fast heat conduction and proper cooling. Another potential source can be erosion of the tungsten electrode and subsequent transfer to the melt pool. This condition also leaves evidence in the form of the eroded electrode surface, though it could be more difficult to detect since proper melting technique results in very minimal damage.
